passages.title: Pixel at the Door
sentences: Sam walked home from school at 3 PM.
Pixel sat by the front door and waited.
Sam opened the door.
Pixel jumped up and barked two times.
He wagged his tail very fast.
Then he ran in circles around Sam.
Sam laughed and hugged his dog.

passages.title: Maya Reads Her Comic
sentences: Maya made a comic about a rock that could talk.
Ms. Ortiz asked her to read it to the class.
Maya stood at the front of the room.
Her hands shook as she held the paper.
She read the first page very quietly.
The class smiled at the funny parts.
Maya read the next page in a loud, clear voice.
At the end, she smiled a big smile.

passages.title: Rain on Match Day
sentences: Ana and Ben had a big soccer match on a Saturday in October.
Ben wanted to score a goal for the first time.
He practiced kicks every day after school.
On Saturday morning, he looked out the window.
Heavy rain was falling on the field.
Then the coach sent a text: "The match is moved to next week."
Ben put his soccer boots back in the closet.
He sat on his bed and looked at the floor for a long time.
Ana sat down next to him.
"We can practice kicks in the garage," she said.
Ben looked up and nodded.

passages.title: Leo's House Key
sentences: Leo came home from the skate park at 5 PM.
He reached into his bag for his house key.
The key was missing.
Leo checked every pocket of his bag two times.
He walked back and forth on the porch.
His mom would be home at 7 PM.
Then Leo looked down at his skateboard.
The key was taped under the board, right where he had put it that morning.
Leo let out a long breath and sat down on the step.
He smiled and opened the door.

passages.title: The Blue Box
sentences: Priya keeps her rover in a blue box on the robotics club shelf.
On Tuesday, she put the rover in the box and went to lunch.
While Priya was at lunch, Ms. Ortiz walked past the shelf.
She saw that the rover's battery light was red.
Ms. Ortiz took the rover out and plugged it in to charge in her office.
She left the blue box empty on the shelf.
After lunch, Priya hurried back to the club room.
She wanted to test the new camera on her rover before the afternoon bell.
She reached for the blue box.

passages.title: The Purple Crystal
sentences: On Monday, Priya was away at a robotics contest in another town.
At lunch, Maya sat at the end of a long table by herself.
She ate her sandwich slowly and looked at the other tables.
Kids were talking and laughing in groups all around her.
Maya opened her sketchbook and drew a purple crystal.
Sam walked by with his tray and stopped.
He leaned in to look at the drawing.
"Is that an amethyst?" he asked.
"I really want to see one up close."
Maya nodded and moved her bag off the seat next to her.
She took a small purple rock out of her pocket and held it out.
Sam sat down, and Maya smiled as they talked about rocks until the bell rang.

passages.title: The Card Tower
sentences: Ben built a tall tower out of playing cards.
It took him a whole hour.
He put the last card on the very top.
Then the family cat jumped onto the table.
The whole tower fell down.
Ben shut his eyes and let out a loud groan.
He pushed all the cards to the side of the table.

passages.title: Ana Gets Ready
sentences: Ana got ready for school on Thursday morning.
She looked out the kitchen window.
The sky over the harbor was dark gray.
Big clouds were moving in from the sea.
Ana put on her coat and zipped it up.
Then she took her yellow umbrella from the hook by the door.
She also put her soccer boots in a plastic bag.
She waved goodbye to Ben and walked to the bus stop.

passages.title: The Green Helmet
sentences: Every day after school, Leo walked past Okafor's Bike Shop on his way to the skate park.
In the front window, there was a bright green helmet with a black stripe.
Leo always stopped and looked at it for a long time.
One day, Leo asked Mr. Okafor how much the helmet cost.
Mr. Okafor told him it was forty dollars.
That night, Leo found an empty jar in the kitchen.
He dropped in the five dollars from his pocket.
On Saturdays, he helped his neighbor wash her car, and every dollar went into the jar.
By the end of the month, the jar was almost full.

passages.title: The Book on Hold
sentences: Sam had waited two weeks for a new library book about the fastest trains in the world.
On Thursday, the library sent a message that said, "Your book is ready to pick up."
After school, Sam ran most of the way to the library.
He walked up to the front desk with a big grin.
The librarian looked through the hold shelf, and then she looked through it again.
"I'm sorry, but I can't find your book," she said.
Sam's grin faded, and his shoulders dropped.
He turned around and walked slowly toward the door.
Then another librarian called his name from the back room.
She held up a book with a silver train on the cover.
Someone had put it on the wrong shelf by mistake.
Sam hurried back to the desk with a huge smile.

passages.title: Maya's Comic on the Wall
sentences: Every spring, the Harbor Town library chooses one comic by a student to hang on the big wall by the front door.
This year, Maya entered a comic about a lighthouse keeper who collects rare crystals.
She worked on it for six weeks, and she redrew the last page three times.
On Monday, a letter from the library arrived at Maya's house.
It said that her comic had been chosen, and that it would hang on the wall for the whole summer.
Maya read the good news twice and pinned the letter above her desk.
She smiled all through dinner and told her mom every detail of the comic again.
After dinner, she noticed one more line at the bottom of the letter, below the signature.
The winner would give a short talk about her comic at the library on Saturday, in front of about forty people.
Maya's smile got smaller, and she began to tap her pencil on the desk.
She liked the idea of so many people seeing her drawings.
But when she pictured herself standing in front of a crowd, her stomach felt tight.
That night, she wrote her talk on three small cards and read it to Priya on a video call.
"It sounds great, and I'll sit in the front row," Priya said.
Maya put the cards in her bag, and her hands were still a little cold.
Then she looked up at the letter above her desk and smiled again.

passages.title: The Big Ramp
sentences: On Saturday, the skate park opened a new ramp that was twice as tall as the old one.
Leo had watched the construction crew build it for a month, and he was the first skater through the gate that morning.
He buckled his helmet, pulled on his knee pads and climbed the steps to the top.
To drop in, a skater stands with the tail of the board on the edge, then leans forward and rolls down the ramp.
From the top, the new ramp looked much steeper than it had from the ground.
Leo set the tail of his board on the edge and put one foot on it.
His legs felt stiff, and his heart was beating fast.
He stood there for a long time, then picked up his board and climbed back down the steps.
At the bottom, he kicked a pebble across the concrete and muttered, "I should be able to do that."
Ana was practicing on the small ramp nearby.
"When I learn a new ramp, I start on a smaller one first," she said.
Leo dropped in on the small ramp ten times, and then on the middle ramp ten more times.
Each time, his legs felt a little less stiff, and his balance felt more steady.
Just before lunch, Leo climbed the steps to the big ramp again.
This time he leaned forward, dropped in and rolled smoothly across to the far side.
He threw both fists in the air and grinned at Ana.

passages.title: The Empty Space on the Board
sentences: Early on Wednesday morning, before any students arrived, Ms. Ortiz stood in front of the science display board.
In the middle hung Maya's comic about how crystals form inside caves, with careful drawings of every stage.
The Harbor Town Science Fair was collecting projects that week, and Ms. Ortiz believed the comic explained crystals more clearly than any poster she had seen.
She unpinned it carefully, slid it into a flat folder and left it in the school office for the fair to collect.
She planned to tell Maya about it at the start of science class, right after lunch.
Maya arrived twenty minutes early, as she usually did, and walked directly to the display board.
Where her comic had been, there were only four empty pins and a pale rectangle on the cork.
Maya stared at the empty space without moving.
She remembered Ms. Ortiz saying that the board was only for the best work in the class.
Her face felt hot, and she walked to her desk without looking at anyone.
All morning, she kept her sketchbook closed, and at lunch she only shrugged when Sam asked about her drawings.
After lunch, Ms. Ortiz began science class with an announcement.
She explained that she had sent Maya's comic to the Harbor Town Science Fair, because it showed how crystals grow better than any poster she had seen.
The class turned to look at Maya, and several students clapped.
Maya's eyes went wide, and then a smile slowly appeared on her face.
After class, she quietly told Ms. Ortiz that she had spent all morning thinking her comic was not good enough.
Ms. Ortiz said she was sorry for the mix-up, and that next time she would leave a note on the board.
As Maya walked back to her desk, her face felt hot again, but this time she was smiling.

passages.title: The Fish Soup
sentences: On Sunday, Ana and Grandma Rose ate lunch at the Lighthouse Café.
Grandma Rose ordered the fish soup for both of them.
Ana had never eaten fish soup before.
She looked down at the bowl and stirred it slowly with her spoon.
She did not take a bite for a long time.
At last, she tasted one small spoonful.
Her eyes opened wide.
Then she ate the whole bowl and asked for more bread to dip in it.
"Can we come back next Sunday?" she asked.

passages.title: The Heron at the Creek
sentences: On Sunday morning, Maya sat on a flat rock beside the creek in Story Woods.
She wanted to draw a great blue heron for her new comic.
A tall blue-gray heron stood very still in the shallow water.
Maya drew its long neck and sharp beak without making a sound.
Then Leo came down the trail with his skateboard under his arm.
"Hey, Maya! What are you drawing?" he called out.
The heron spread its wide wings and flew away down the creek.
Maya looked at her half-finished drawing and pressed her lips together.
She did not answer Leo.
Leo looked at the empty water, and then he looked at Maya's page.
He sat down on the rock next to her without another word.
They waited together in silence for twenty minutes.
Then the heron landed in the same spot, and Maya finished its wings.
She turned the sketchbook so Leo could see it, and he gave her a thumbs-up.

passages.title: Closed for Cleaning
sentences: Ben had read every dinosaur book in the Harbor Town library.
On Saturday, Grandma Rose took Ben and Sam to the big museum in the city by train.
Ben wanted to see one thing most of all: a full Triceratops skeleton with all three horns.
When they reached the Dinosaur Hall, a rope hung across the doorway.
A sign on the rope said, "Closed today for cleaning."
Ben stopped and stared at the sign, and his shoulders dropped.
Just then, a woman in a blue work shirt walked over with a box of soft brushes.
She said they could stand by the doorway and watch her clean the skeleton.
She brushed dust from its horns while Ben watched every move.
Ben asked her eleven questions, one after another.
On the train home, he talked about the brushes all the way to Harbor Town.

passages.title: The Last Block
sentences: Ben had played the same video game level all afternoon.
It was the hardest level in the game, with a long bridge of moving blocks.
At five o'clock, he finally jumped onto the very last block.
Just then, Ana walked past the TV with a basket of laundry.
Her foot caught the console's power cord, and the screen went black.
Ben dropped his controller on the couch and covered his face with both hands.
Ana's cheeks turned red, and she said quietly, "I'm so sorry."
She plugged the cord back in and stood very still while the game loaded.
A message appeared on the screen: "Progress saved at the last block."
Ben let out a long breath and picked up his controller.
Ana smiled for the first time and sat down to watch him finish.

passages.title: The Closed Bridge
sentences: For a whole week, Sam planned a Saturday hike to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
He spread his trail map across the kitchen table and carefully traced the route with a green pencil.
The route crossed the creek on a wooden footbridge, climbed steadily through the pine forest and reached the lookout in about two hours.
On an index card, he calculated the time for each section: start at 9:00, footbridge at 9:20, lookout at 11:00.
Every evening that week, he studied the card again and smiled.
Leo and Maya were coming, and so was Pixel.
On Saturday morning, a yellow sign stood in front of the footbridge.
It said, "Bridge closed for repairs. Please use another trail."
Sam gripped the map so tightly that the paper crinkled.
"Now the whole plan is wrong," he said in a loud, sharp voice.
He turned away from his friends and kicked at the gravel.
Maya waited quietly, and Leo held Pixel's leash.
After a minute, Sam took three slow breaths, the way he did at school when a plan changed.
Then he unfolded the map on a flat rock and studied it again.
Another trail followed the creek upstream to a stone bridge near the old mill, then joined his original route on the opposite side.
The detour would add approximately thirty minutes.
Sam crossed out the old times on his card and wrote new ones underneath.
The three friends reached the lookout at 11:30 instead of 11:00.
Sam ate his sandwich on the bench while Pixel leaned against his leg.
Then he drew the mill trail on his map in blue pencil, so he would know it next time.
"I liked the stone bridge," he told Maya. "We should go that way again."

passages.title: The Open Door
sentences: Every Thursday at 4:45 PM, the Harbor Middle School jazz band, which has players from every grade, rehearsed in the music room at the end of the east hallway.
Leo's usual route to the skate park passed directly by its open door.
Each week, he slowed down when he heard the jazz drummer practicing a complicated swing rhythm.
Sometimes he paused at the water fountain and quietly tapped the beat on his skateboard with two fingers.
One Thursday, Ms. Gray, the music teacher, noticed him and stepped into the hallway.
"Your swing rhythm is very steady," she said. "Have you ever played jazz?"
Leo shrugged and answered, "Not really. Jazz is kind of complicated anyway."
Then he glanced past Ms. Gray at the shiny drum set for a long moment before he continued down the hallway.
That evening, Leo watched video lessons about jazz drumming until his mother reminded him to turn off the light.
The following Thursday, Ms. Gray was waiting by the door with a pair of wire brushes, which jazz drummers use for a soft sound.
"The jazz band needs a second drummer," she explained. "Would you like to try a simple swing beat?"
Leo held the brushes and stared at the floor for a second.
His cheeks felt warm, but he could not stop grinning.
He sat down behind the drum set and played a steady swing beat, and his hands trembled only a little.
When he finished, two members of the jazz band applauded.
Leo laughed and said, "That was more fun than I expected."
Then he asked Ms. Gray what time rehearsal started the following week.

passages.title: The Empty Stairs
sentences: The Harbor Beach clean-up was at nine o'clock on Saturday morning, and Ana had marked it on her calendar three weeks earlier.
Volunteers would pick up plastic bottles, fishing line and other trash before the tide could carry it out to sea.
Ana cared about this because she had read that sea turtles sometimes mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish, which they eat.
The notice from school said to meet at the north stairs, next to the lifeguard tower.
Ana arrived at 8:50 with her gloves and a bucket, but the north stairs were empty.
She took out her phone to check the group chat, but the screen stayed black, because she had forgotten to charge it.
She waited until 9:15, and then until 9:25, watching the empty sand in both directions.
"They must have canceled it," she thought. "And nobody remembered to tell me."
She sat down on the bottom step and pulled her knees up to her chin.
Ana did not know that a message had been sent to the group chat the night before.
A storm had washed a long line of seaweed and trash onto the south end of the beach, so the volunteers would meet there instead.
From the north stairs, a curve in the shore and a row of sand dunes hid the south end from view.
At 9:30, Ana stood up and started to walk home along the water.
As she came around the curve, she saw about thirty people in yellow vests, bending to pick up trash.
Ms. Ortiz waved both arms and called her name, and Ana started to run.
When Ms. Ortiz explained about the message, Ana's cheeks turned pink, and she laughed and shook her head.
Then she pulled on her gloves and filled her bucket with bottle caps and tangled fishing line.
By noon, the volunteers had filled forty bags, and Ana walked home tired, sandy and smiling.

passages.title: Clouds over the Dome
sentences: For an entire month, Priya had been crossing days off her calendar until Star Night at the Lantern Peaks Observatory.
On Star Night, visitors could look through the enormous telescope inside the white dome on the hilltop.
Priya especially wanted to see the rings of Saturn with her own eyes, not just in photographs on a screen.
She and Sam rode the evening bus up the winding road with a thermos of hot chocolate and Sam's folded star chart.
By the time they arrived, thick gray clouds had drifted in and covered the entire sky.
A staff member at the entrance explained that the telescope could not see through clouds, so there would be no viewing that night.
Priya stopped smiling and crossed her arms tightly.
"We waited a whole month for this," she said in a flat voice, and she turned back toward the bus stop.
Sam was disappointed too, but he noticed a small sign beside the staircase: "Cloudy Night Tour of the Telescope, 8:00."
He showed it to Priya, and after a long pause, she uncrossed her arms and followed him up the stairs.
Inside the dome, an astronomer named Dr. Hale showed them the gigantic curved mirror that collects light from distant stars and galaxies.
Then she pressed a button, and the whole roof of the dome rotated slowly with a deep rumble.
Priya asked how the motors could possibly move something so heavy, and Dr. Hale opened a metal panel so she could examine the gears.
Before they left, Dr. Hale explained that their tickets would still be valid on the next clear Friday.
On the bus home, Priya wrote "Next clear Friday" at the top of the star chart.
She kept glancing up at the cloudy sky through the window.
But she was smiling, and she described the gears to Sam for most of the ride down the hill.

passages.title: After the Rain
sentences: Rain fell on Harbor Town all morning.
Then the sun came out.
Ana looked out the kitchen window.
A big rainbow was over the harbor!
Ana gasped and put her hands on her cheeks.
She ran to get her brother Ben.
"Come and see!" she shouted.
Ben ran to the window and grinned.

passages.title: The Giant Footprint
sentences: Ben went to the museum with his class.
He saw a dinosaur footprint in a big rock.
Ben put his shoe next to the footprint.
The footprint was three times as long as his shoe!
Ben's eyes got big.
"Wow!" he said.
Then he took a photo of his shoe and the footprint.
He showed the photo to every kid on the bus home.

passages.title: A Bark at the Dock
sentences: Priya walked on the dock by the harbor.
She heard a loud bark.
She looked for a dog, but there was no dog.
Then she saw a brown sea lion on a rock!
Priya gasped and pointed at it.
The sea lion looked at her.
Then it slid into the water with a big splash.
Priya laughed and waved goodbye.

passages.title: The Late Train
sentences: Sam went to the station to see the new blue express train.
It was supposed to arrive at 4:00 PM.
He waited beside the departure board with his notebook.
At 4:00 PM, the board changed.
It said, "Blue express: 30 minutes late."
Sam stamped his foot.
"That was not the plan!" he said in a loud voice.
He sat on a bench and frowned at the board.
After a minute, he opened his notebook.
He wrote down every train that went by while he waited.
He counted two long freight trains and one fast passenger train.
At 4:30 PM, the blue express finally rolled in.
Sam smiled and carefully drew it at the top of a new page.

passages.title: The Pancake Flip
sentences: On Sunday morning, Ben made pancakes for the whole family.
He wanted to flip one high in the air, like a chef on television.
He gave the pan a big push.
The pancake flew up and landed on the kitchen floor.
Ben's face turned red, and he looked down at his shoes.
Ana laughed loudly at first.
Then she noticed Ben's face, and she stopped laughing.
"My first flip landed on the floor too," she said.
Ben looked up and grinned.
His next pancake landed perfectly back in the pan.

passages.title: The Waving Robot
sentences: Priya built a robot arm at robotics club.
On Friday, she was going to show it to her class.
That morning, she checked the batteries three times.
Her hands felt cold as she set the arm on the table.
She pressed the button.
The arm lifted up and waved at Ms. Ortiz.
Ms. Ortiz waved back, and the whole class laughed and clapped.
Priya stood up tall and smiled a wide smile.
"Next, I will teach it to shake hands," she said.

passages.title: Priya's Cello Chat
sentences: Priya and Maya sent these messages on Tuesday night.

rows: Priya: I practiced my new cello piece for an hour.
Priya: I still miss the same three notes in the fast part. I want to put my cello away and never play that part again.
Maya: Try that part very slowly first. It helps me on my flute.
Priya: OK. I will try it at half speed.
Priya: It is 8:00 now. I played the fast part slowly five times with no mistakes!
Priya: Then I played it fast. No mistakes again!
Maya: You did it! Will you play it for me at lunch tomorrow?

passages.title: Hail at the Bus Stop
sentences: Ben and Maya waited at the bus stop after school.
All at once, small balls of ice began to fall from the sky.
It was hail!
The hailstones were as small as peas, and they bounced on the road.
Ben and Maya hurried under the bus shelter.
Ben held out his hand and caught three hailstones.
"Look how perfectly round they are!" he said with a big grin.
Maya did not look.
She held her sketchbook tightly against her chest and frowned at its wet cover.
Ben noticed her face.
He took off his baseball cap and placed it over the sketchbook.
Maya smiled at him, and then she looked at the hailstones too.

passages.title: Stars on the Ceiling
sentences: Sam bought a pack of glow-in-the-dark stars for his bedroom ceiling.
He wanted to make the Big Dipper, a group of seven bright stars in the night sky.
Four stars make the bowl of the Big Dipper, and the rest make its long handle.
Sam looked at his star chart and stuck each star up with care.
That evening, Leo came over to play video games.
Sam turned off the light and pointed at the ceiling.
"The handle of the Big Dipper has three stars, not four," Leo said.
Sam's smile disappeared.
"No, it has four," he said, and he crossed his arms.
Then he turned on the light and opened his star chart.
He counted the handle stars with his finger: one, two, three.
Sam's cheeks turned pink, and he laughed a little.
"You're right," he said.
Leo held the chair while Sam took down the extra star.
Now there were exactly seven stars, and Sam turned off the light again with a grin.

passages.title: Paper or Phone
sentences: On Saturday, Ben and Maya hiked to the waterfall in Story Woods.
Ben used the map on his phone, and Maya carried a paper trail map in her pocket.
Ben liked how a blue dot on his phone showed exactly where they were.
At a fork in the trail, Ben looked down at his phone, and the screen went black.
The battery was empty.
Ben stopped walking and looked left, and then right.
"Which way do we go?" he asked in a quiet voice.
Maya unfolded her paper map on a tree stump.
She found the fork and traced the left trail to the waterfall with her finger.
"Left," she said calmly.
Twenty minutes later, they heard the loud rush of the waterfall.
Ben let out a long breath and smiled.
On the way home, he asked Maya to show him how to read the paper map.

passages.title: Just Gray and Brown
sentences: Maya invited Ana to the rock club at the mine museum on a Saturday in March.
Ana went, but she did not expect to have much fun.
"Rocks are just gray and brown," she told Ben before she left.
At the museum, Mr. Varga led the club into a small room with no windows.
Rows of plain, dull rocks sat on the shelves.
Ana yawned and leaned against the wall.
Then Mr. Varga switched off the lights and turned on a special lamp.
He explained that some minerals glow in bright colors under this kind of lamp.
All at once, the dull rocks glowed bright green, red and blue.
Ana stood up straight, and her mouth opened wide.
She walked along every shelf and asked Mr. Varga the name of each glowing mineral.
On the way home, she asked Maya when the next club meeting was.

passages.title: The Puzzle Door
sentences: Ana and Leo played a puzzle game at Ana's house.
To open the last door, a player had to light four lamps in the right order.
Ana tried again and again, but the door stayed shut.
She pressed the controller buttons hard and groaned.
Leo had already finished this level at home, so he knew the right order.
He opened his mouth, and then he closed it again.
He sat on his hands and watched.
"Look at the colors on the wall," he said quietly.
Ana looked at the wall and saw four colored stripes.
She lit the lamps in the same order as the stripes, and the door slid open.
Ana jumped up and cheered.
Leo grinned and gave her a high five.

passages.title: Goalie for a Day
sentences: Ben always played forward, because he loved chasing the ball and shooting at the goal.
Before Saturday's game, Coach Novak called him over.
"Our goalie is visiting her grandparents this weekend," the coach said. "Can you play in goal today?"
Ben looked at the ground and did not answer for a long moment.
Then he nodded once, without a smile.
He pulled on the big goalie gloves very slowly.
For most of the first half, he stood in front of the net with his arms crossed.
Then a player from the other team kicked a hard, low shot.
Ben dove to his left and stopped the ball with both hands.
His teammates ran over and cheered.
After that, Ben clapped his gloves together before every kick.
After the game, he asked Coach Novak if he could practice in goal again next week.

passages.title: The Bean Seeds
sentences: Priya planted six bean seeds in the school garden on Monday.
The packet said the first sprouts would come up in one to two weeks.
Priya checked the soil every morning before class.
After eight days, the soil was still flat and brown.
Priya frowned and poked the dirt with one finger.
"I think my seeds are bad," she told Ms. Ortiz.
Ms. Ortiz explained that cold nights can make seeds grow more slowly.
She told Priya to wait a few more days.
On the eleventh day, Priya saw a tiny green loop pushing up through the soil.
She knelt down so fast that her backpack slid off her shoulder.
By the end of the week, all six seeds had sprouted, and Priya started a chart to measure them every day.

passages.title: Keeping Time
sentences: Ben wanted to play a song on his keyboard with a drummer, just like a real band.
Leo, the drummer in the Grade 7 band, came over after school with his practice pad and sticks.
They started the song together.
By the end of the first page, Ben was playing faster and faster.
Leo stopped drumming and said, "You sped up."
Ben pushed back his chair and let out a loud sigh.
"I always do that," he said, staring at the keys.
Leo tapped his sticks together four times and counted out loud, "One, two, three, four."
"Listen to my sticks, not your fingers," he said.
They started again, and this time Ben kept his eyes on Leo's sticks.
They reached the last note at exactly the same moment.
Ben spun around on his chair and laughed.
"Can we record that one?" he asked.

passages.title: Pixel Meets the Rover
sentences: Priya brought her rover to Sam's house to test it on his long hallway floor.
She set it down and pressed the start button.
The rover rolled forward with a soft whirring sound.
Pixel had been asleep on his mat, but now he lifted his head.
When the rover rolled toward him, Pixel jumped up and backed away.
His ears went flat, and he gave a short, low bark.
Priya stopped the rover right away.
"He has never seen a robot before," Sam said, and he knelt next to Pixel.
Priya left the rover sitting still on the floor.
After a minute, Pixel crept closer and sniffed its wheels.
Then he sniffed the blinking light on top.
His tail began to wag, slowly at first and then faster.
"I think he likes it now," Priya said with a laugh.

passages.title: The Red Pie
sentences: When Sam came into Rose's Bakery after school, a pie was cooling on the back counter.
Red juice bubbled up through the holes in its top crust.
Sam's favorite pie in the whole world was cherry.
He dropped his backpack and hurried over to the counter.
"Is that a cherry pie?" he asked, but Grandma Rose was busy with a customer and only waved.
Sam grinned and took two plates from the shelf.
Then Grandma Rose cut the pie, and Sam saw pink and green pieces inside.
It was strawberry and rhubarb, not cherry.
Sam's grin faded a little.
"Rhubarb is a sour stalk, but the strawberries make it sweet," Grandma Rose said.
Sam took a small bite and chewed slowly.
Then he took a much bigger bite.
"Can I have a second piece?" he asked.

passages.title: Second Prize
sentences: Every year, the Harbor Town railway holds an essay contest for students who love trains.
The first prize is a ride in the driver's cab of the morning express, right beside the driver.
Sam spent three weekends on his essay about how the express climbs the steep hill into Lantern Peaks.
He read it aloud to Pixel so many times that he could recite the first paragraph from memory.
On Friday, an envelope arrived from the railway.
Sam opened it in the hallway and read the first line: "Congratulations! You have won second prize."
Second prize was a guided tour of the train yard and the repair shop.
Sam read the letter again, slowly, and his shoulders sank a little.
"Second prize is really good," his dad said with a smile. "Are you happy?"
"Yes," Sam said quietly, and he folded the letter into a small, tight square.
That night, he looked at a photo of the express on his wall for a long time before he turned off the light.
On the morning of the tour, a guide led Sam through the enormous repair shop.
Mechanics were replacing a wheel on a locomotive, and Sam asked so many questions that the guide laughed.
Near the end of the tour, the guide noticed Sam staring at a parked locomotive.
She opened the cab door and let him sit in the driver's seat for five minutes, with the engine switched off.
Sam rested his hands on the controls without moving them, and he grinned the whole time.
On the walk home, he told his dad that he had already chosen the topic for next year's essay.

passages.title: Cards Face Up
sentences: On Friday evening, Maya went to Ana and Ben's house for game night.
The twins had a new card game in which players race to fill their boats with fish cards before anyone else.
Ana and Ben had played it twenty times, but Maya had never seen the rules.
Ben explained them very quickly, and Maya nodded as if she understood.
Maya lost the first round, and then the second round, by a lot.
Each time Ana won, she cheered and slapped the table.
Maya laughed along, but her laugh was short, and then she stopped talking.
She held her cards close to her face and kept pressing their edges with her thumbs.
When Ana asked if she wanted to play again, Maya said, "Sure, it's fine," without looking up.
Ben watched Maya for a moment.
"Let's play the next round with our cards face up," he suggested. "That's how Ana and I learned, and we can show each other our best moves."
Maya's shoulders relaxed, and she laid her cards on the table.
With the cards face up, she soon noticed that the twins saved their biggest fish cards for the end.
In the fourth round, with the cards hidden again, Maya filled her boat first.
She threw both hands in the air, and this time her laugh was long and loud.

passages.title: The Question in the Sketchbook
sentences: On Saturday morning, Mr. Varga guided the rock club through the Ridgeway Mine Museum in Lantern Peaks.
He showed them a narrow tunnel where miners once dug for copper, a row of heavy iron carts and a wall of glittering mineral samples.
Maya stayed near the back of the group with her sketchbook open, drawing everything.
At the end of each room, Mr. Varga asked, "Any questions?"
In the mineral room, Maya noticed a bright green stone covered in curving light and dark stripes.
She took a step toward Mr. Varga, then stopped and looked at the floor.
When he asked for questions, two other kids spoke first, and Maya's hand rose halfway before it dropped back to her side.
Then her pencil moved quickly across a fresh page of her sketchbook.
Sam was standing beside her, and he saw what she had written: "What is the green striped stone, and why does it have stripes?"
"You could show him the page," Sam whispered.
Maya held her sketchbook against her chest for a second.
Then she walked up and turned the page toward Mr. Varga without a word.
He read it, and his eyebrows went up.
"Excellent question," he said. "That stone is malachite. It forms inside copper mines one thin layer at a time, and each layer makes a stripe."
Maya wrote down every word, and she smiled at Sam all the way to the bus.

passages.title: Five Strings
sentences: On the first Friday of every month, the Lighthouse Café holds a music night, and anyone can sign up to play one song.
Sam had practiced his guitar song every evening for three weeks, and he was fourth on Mrs. Lin's list.
Grandma Rose and his dad sat at a table near the front, and Leo waited outside the window with Pixel.
While the third player was singing, Sam tuned his guitar one last time.
As he tightened the thinnest string, it snapped with a sharp twang.
Sam stared at the loose string curling in the air.
His face went hot, and he gripped the neck of the guitar so hard that his knuckles turned white.
"Now I can't play it," he whispered. "I practiced it with six strings."
He thought about walking straight out the door.
Mrs. Lin knelt beside him and quietly asked if he wanted to wait until the end of the night.
Sam took three slow breaths and thought carefully about his song.
Most of his chords used the thicker strings, and he could hum the high notes instead of playing them.
He told Mrs. Lin that he would try it with five strings, as long as he could go last.
When his turn came, his first chord sounded a little thin, but the second one sounded steady.
He hummed the high part, and a few people at the back hummed along.
When he finished, everyone clapped, and Grandma Rose stood up from her chair.
Sam bowed, and then he laughed and held up the broken string for everyone to see.

passages.title: The Dropped Baton
sentences: On Field Day, the four fastest runners from each class competed in the relay race, passing a short metal baton from one runner to the next.
Ana ran third for her class, and Priya ran last.
They had practiced the handoff every lunch period for a week: Ana would shout "Now!" and Priya would reach back without turning around.
When the starting whistle blew, Ana's class quickly moved into second place.
Ana sprinted down the track and shouted, "Now!"
Priya reached back, but the baton hit her fingers and bounced onto the grass.
Ana grabbed it and pushed it into Priya's hand, and Priya raced away, but two runners had already passed her.
Their class finished fourth out of five.
Ana walked off the track with her eyes fixed on her shoes.
Across the field, Priya was talking seriously with Ms. Ortiz, and she was not smiling.
Ana was certain that Priya was angry with her, so she sat alone under a maple tree and did not go over.
A few minutes later, Priya jogged over and sat down beside her.
"I was asking Ms. Ortiz about our handoff," Priya said. "I think I reached back too early."
Ana looked up. "You're not mad at me?"
"No! I'm glad we finished, and I want to practice the handoff again for next year," Priya said.
Ana let out a long breath, and the two friends walked to the water table together.

passages.title: The Bird Count
sentences: Every winter, volunteers all over the island count the birds they see on one weekend, so that scientists can learn which kinds of birds are doing well.
Maya signed up to count birds along the creek in Story Woods, and she asked Priya to come with her.
Maya brought binoculars, a bird guide and a clipboard with a tally sheet.
The morning was gray and very cold, and frost covered the grass beside the trail.
Maya spotted a chickadee within the first minute and marked it on her sheet with a big grin.
Priya stood with her hands pushed deep into her pockets.
She kept bouncing on her toes, and every few minutes she glanced back toward the parking lot.
When Maya asked if she was having fun, Priya said, "Sure," but her teeth were chattering.
Maya looked at Priya's red nose and at her shoulders pulled up toward her ears.
She poured hot cocoa from her thermos and handed Priya the cup.
"Can you be our tally keeper?" she asked. "You can stand in the sunny spot by the bridge."
Priya wrapped both hands around the warm cup and moved into the patch of sunlight.
A few minutes later, a blue and white bird dove straight into the creek and flew up with a tiny fish.
"What was that?" Priya shouted, nearly spilling her cocoa.
Maya found the page in the bird guide: it was a belted kingfisher.
For the rest of the morning, Priya held the clipboard and watched the water for another one.

passages.title: The Copy in the Hall
sentences: On Saturday morning, Leo and Priya rode the bus to the Harbor Town museum.
In the main hall stood a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton so tall that its skull nearly touched the ceiling.
Leo walked around it three times, staring up at the long rows of teeth.
"I can't believe these are the actual bones," he whispered to Priya. "This animal really stood here."
Dr. Bell, the museum's paleontologist, overheard him and smiled.
She explained that the skeleton in the hall was a cast, an exact copy made from real fossils.
Real fossil bones are heavy and fragile, so many museums keep them safe in storage and display copies instead.
Leo stopped smiling and took a step back from the skeleton.
"So it's fake," he said in a flat voice, and he pushed his hands into his pockets.
Dr. Bell invited them downstairs to her laboratory and opened a wooden drawer.
Inside, on a bed of soft foam, lay a single dark tooth as long as a banana.
"This one is real," she said. "It is about sixty-seven million years old."
She handed Leo a pair of gloves and let him hold the tooth for ten seconds.
Leo held his breath, and his hands stayed completely still.
On the bus home, he asked Priya to quiz him on dinosaur facts until they reached their stop.

passages.title: The Touch Tank
sentences: On Sunday afternoon, Ben and Maya visited the marine science center at the end of the harbor.
In the middle of the main room was a wide, shallow touch tank full of sea stars, hermit crabs and sea urchins.
A volunteer explained the rule: visitors could gently touch the animals with two fingers, but they could never lift them out of the water.
Maya rolled up her sleeve right away and touched a purple sea star.
"It feels rough and bumpy," she said.
Ben stood a step back from the edge with his hands behind his back.
"I don't want to bother them," he joked. "They look very busy."
When a hermit crab scuttled toward his side of the tank, Ben laughed loudly, but he took another step back.
Maya noticed that he still had not touched a single animal.
"Want to try the sea star with me?" Maya asked quietly. "It moves so slowly that you can watch it the whole time."
Ben looked at the sea star for a long moment.
Then he put his fingertips into the cold water next to Maya's hand.
He touched one arm of the sea star, and his eyebrows went up.
"It's rough!" he said. "I thought it would be slimy."
He touched it twice more before they moved on, and on the way out he asked the volunteer exactly how sea stars eat.

passages.title: The Moving Light
sentences: Priya read that the International Space Station would pass over Harbor Town at 7:42 PM on Thursday.
The station circles Earth about every ninety minutes, and from the ground it looks like a very bright star moving smoothly across the sky.
Priya invited Leo to watch it with her from the field behind her house.
Leo arrived at 7:30 with a flashlight and a bag of popcorn.
"Nobody can know the exact minute," he said with a grin. "You're just guessing, right?"
Priya did not argue.
She checked her watch, pointed at the trees in the west and waited calmly.
At 7:41, Leo was tossing popcorn into the air and catching it in his mouth.
"See? Nothing," he said.
At 7:42, a bright, steady light rose over the treetops, exactly where Priya was pointing.
It did not blink like an airplane, and it moved silently across the whole sky.
Leo stopped moving, with a piece of popcorn halfway to his mouth.
"There are astronauts living inside that," Priya said softly.
They watched without talking until the light faded in the east, about five minutes later.
Then Leo turned to Priya and asked when the station would pass over again.

passages.title: A Night in the Dinosaur Hall
sentences: Once a year, the Harbor Town museum invites twenty students to spend a night sleeping on the floor of its Dinosaur Hall.
Ben had applied three years in a row, and this spring his name was finally drawn, along with Maya's.
He packed his sleeping bag a full week early and taped a list of every skeleton in the hall to the inside of his bedroom door.
Maya packed her sketchbook, a flashlight and two extra pairs of socks.
At nine o'clock, the staff switched off the main lights, and the hall filled with long, unfamiliar shadows.
The Triceratops skull above their sleeping bags seemed much larger in the dark than it had during the day.
Ben sat straight up and whispered, "This is the best night of my entire life."
Maya zipped her sleeping bag up to her chin and kept her flashlight switched on, pointed at the ceiling.
Whenever the old building creaked, her eyes darted toward the sound.
"Are you okay?" Ben asked.
"I'm just tired," Maya answered, but she did not close her eyes.
A few minutes later, Dr. Bell came by with a lantern and offered a short night tour to anyone who was still awake.
Ben jumped up immediately, and after a moment, Maya slowly unzipped her bag and followed.
Dr. Bell held her lantern close to each skeleton and explained what the animal ate, how fast it might have moved and where its bones had been discovered.
She also pointed out small details that most visitors never notice, such as the rough bumps where powerful muscles were once attached to the bones.
Maya began to sketch by lantern light, and her drawing hand grew steadier with every skeleton.
When they returned to their sleeping bags, Maya switched off her flashlight without being asked.
"The shadows are just the skeletons," she told Ben. "I know every one of them now."
She fell asleep before Ben did, with her sketchbook open beside her pillow.

passages.title: The Cake Without Eggs
sentences: Grandma Rose bakes cakes for half of Harbor Town, but nobody ever bakes a cake for her.
This year, Sam decided to surprise her on her birthday with her favorite dessert: chocolate cake with chocolate frosting.
He copied her own recipe onto an index card, bought the ingredients with his allowance and hid them at the back of the refrigerator.
His plan was to bake the cake on Sunday morning while Grandma Rose was at her walking group, then carry it to the bakery at noon.
On Sunday morning, Sam lined up everything on the counter and read the card again.
The first line said, "Two eggs."
He opened the egg carton and found it empty, because his dad had made omelets the night before.
Sam slammed the carton shut and pressed both hands flat against the counter.
"The whole plan is ruined," he said, with his teeth pressed together.
The grocery store did not open until noon, and he could not ask Grandma Rose for eggs without spoiling the surprise.
Sam walked to the window and counted ten slow breaths, the way he did at school when a plan changed.
Then he remembered an old cookbook on his dad's shelf that Grandma Rose had once shown him, full of recipes from times when eggs were difficult to find.
One recipe was a chocolate cake made with vinegar and baking soda instead of eggs.
When vinegar and baking soda mix, they make tiny bubbles of gas that help the batter rise.
Sam took the cookbook down, crossed out "Two eggs" on his card and wrote the new steps underneath.
The cake came out of the oven a little flat on one side, so Sam covered that side with extra frosting.
At noon, he carried it into the bakery, and Grandma Rose put both hands over her mouth.
After her first bite, she asked for the recipe, and Sam explained the vinegar trick with a proud grin.
"I think I like this one even better than mine," she said.

passages.title: Too Fast
sentences: Ms. Gray asked Priya and Sam to play a duet at the library's spring music night, with Priya on cello and Sam on guitar.
They chose a slow, gentle folk song and practiced it twice a week in the music room after school.
At every practice, Sam started a little faster than the time before.
He liked the song best when it felt lively, and he tapped his foot hard to keep himself going.
Priya's part had a long run of low notes in the middle, and at Sam's speed her fingers could barely keep up.
Each time they reached that section, she frowned at the music, and her bow made a scratchy sound.
When they finished, Sam would grin and say, "That was our best one yet!"
Priya always nodded and said, "Yeah, good," and then she packed up her cello faster than usual.
One evening, Sam noticed that she had marked the middle section of her music with a pencil arrow and the word "SLOWER."
Until then, Sam had believed that the song was going perfectly, because Priya had never said that anything was wrong.
Now he remembered her frowns, her scratchy notes and how quickly she always left.
"Is the middle part too fast for you?" he asked.
Priya let out a long breath and admitted that she had wanted to ask him to slow down for two weeks, but she had worried that he would think she was not good enough.
Sam said he would much rather play together than play fast.
They tried the song again while Priya tapped the speed she wanted with her foot, and this time her low notes came out smooth and warm.
At the music night, the audience was so quiet during the middle section that Sam could hear the cello's lowest notes humming through the floor.
Afterward, Priya told Sam that it was the first time she had truly enjoyed playing the song.

passages.title: The Long Download
sentences: For a month, Ben and Leo had counted down the days until a new racing game came out on Saturday at ten in the morning.
They planned to download it at Leo's house the moment it was released and play until dinner.
Ben arrived at 9:45 with a bag of pretzels and a list of the tracks he wanted to try first.
At ten o'clock, Leo pressed the download button, and a gray bar appeared on the screen.
Underneath it, small letters said, "Time remaining: 8 hours."
So many people were downloading the game at the same moment that every download had slowed down.
Ben groaned, dropped onto the couch and stared at the bar.
Every few minutes he got up to check it, and every time he sat back down a little harder.
Leo only shrugged and said, "It will finish when it finishes," and then he went to the kitchen for juice.
Leo's little brother, who is eight years old, wandered in holding a board game about building railroads across a map.
"Will you play this with me?" he asked.
Ben opened his mouth to say no, and then he looked at the gray bar again.
"One game," he said with a sigh, and he sat down on the floor.
The game was harder than it looked, because every player had to plan a route between cities while the others blocked the best tracks.
By the second game, Ben was leaning over the board, counting spaces and cheerfully arguing about the rules.
At six o'clock, the download finished with a loud chime.
Leo grabbed the controllers, but Ben did not move from the floor.
"Can we finish this round first?" he asked. "I'm about to complete my longest route."
Leo laughed, and his little brother grinned so widely that he nearly knocked over the board.

passages.title: The Robot Workshop
sentences: Every Saturday in March, the Harbor Town library held a robot workshop for younger children, and Mrs. Hall asked Priya to help as a volunteer.
Priya spent Friday evening preparing six small robot kits, each with wheels, a motor, a battery pack and a simple remote control.
She was excited to show the children how a handful of parts could become a machine that moved.
On Saturday, five of the six children opened their kits immediately and started snapping pieces together.
The sixth child, a boy of about eight in a striped sweater, sat with his arms folded and his kit still closed.
When Priya asked if he wanted help, he shook his head and looked out the window.
Priya decided that he must think robots were boring, so she left him alone and spent the hour helping the others.
As the children packed up, the boy walked over to the table where the finished robots were racing, and he watched them closely.
He reached out to touch one of the wheels, then quickly pulled his hand back.
Mrs. Hall knelt beside him and spoke quietly with him for a minute.
Afterward, she told Priya that the boy loved robots, but he had never built anything before and was worried that he would break the parts.
Priya's cheeks felt warm, because she had guessed wrong.
She opened a spare kit, sat down next to the boy and said, "I broke my first motor too. That's how I learned where the wires go."
She let him hold each part before he connected it, and she never touched his robot unless he asked her to.
Twenty minutes later, his robot rolled across the floor, and he turned to Priya with an enormous smile.
"Can I come back next Saturday?" he asked.

passages.title: Learning to Sail
sentences: In July, Ana and Leo signed up for a week of sailing lessons in the calm water inside the harbor.
Every student wore a life jacket, and a safety boat with a motor followed the small sailboats wherever they went.
On the first morning, Ana and Leo shared a boat with their instructor, a tall woman with a whistle who had been sailing for thirty years.
As soon as the wind filled the sail, the boat tipped to one side, and the edge dipped close to the water.
Leo whooped, leaned out over the side and laughed into the wind.
Ana grabbed the bench with both hands, and her knuckles turned pale.
She stared at the water rushing past and did not say a word for several minutes.
"Is it supposed to lean like this?" she finally asked in a small voice.
The instructor explained that a sailboat leans whenever the wind pushes on its sail.
She said their boat had a heavy fin called a keel under the water, which pulls the boat back upright.
Then she handed Ana the rope that controls the sail.
When Ana let the rope out a little, the boat leaned less and slowed down.
When she pulled it back in, the sail filled again, and the boat leaned and went faster.
Ana tried it again and again, and her shoulders slowly dropped away from her ears.
By the end of the lesson, Ana was the one asking to go faster.
As they sailed back toward the dock, Leo asked her to teach him the rope trick.
Ana explained it carefully, holding the rope exactly the way the instructor had shown her, and she grinned the whole way in.

passages.title: Two Names on the Board
sentences: At the end of the first practice of the season, Coach Novak asked the soccer team to vote for a captain.
Each player wrote one name on a slip of paper and dropped it into an empty water bottle, and the coach wrote the totals on a whiteboard.
Ben had hoped to become captain since the previous season, and he had already imagined exactly how he would lead the warm-up exercises.
When the counting finished, two names were on the board: Ben had six votes, and Ana had nine.
The team cheered enthusiastically, and several players patted Ana on the back.
Ben clapped too, and he was the first one to hug his sister.
"You'll be great at it," he told her, and he meant it.
But on the walk home, Ben kicked a pebble along the sidewalk for three entire blocks and answered Ana's questions with single words.
Ana noticed how quiet her brother was.
She was excited about becoming captain, but she kept glancing sideways at Ben, and her smile kept fading.
That night, she knocked on his door and asked if he would lead the warm-ups at every practice, since he already knew every stretch without looking at a list.
Ben looked up from his game controller.
"You would really want me to do that?" he asked.
Ana explained that a good captain should choose the best person for each responsibility.
At the next practice, Ben stood confidently in front of the team and led the warm-ups in a loud, clear voice.
Ana stretched in the front row along with everyone else, and she grinned at him when they finished.
On the walk home that afternoon, Ben talked the entire way.

passages.title: Junior Rangers
sentences: In August, Leo spent a week at the Junior Ranger day camp in Story Woods, where children learn to identify trees, follow animal tracks and care for the trails.
His friends were all away or busy that week, so he did not know a single person in his group of twelve.
On Monday morning, he tried to make the group laugh with one of his best jokes.
Nobody laughed, and a few kids glanced at him for a second before they went back to their conversations.
On Monday and Tuesday, Leo hiked at the very back of the line.
At lunch, he ate his sandwich on a log a little apart from the others and kept his eyes on his trail guide.
When the ranger asked everyone to find a partner for the tracking game, the others paired up quickly, and Leo was left standing alone.
He shrugged and told the ranger it was fine, because he liked working by himself.
But on Tuesday evening, he told his mom that he did not want to go back.
On Wednesday, the ranger set a challenge: each team had to build a small bridge across a muddy stream using only fallen branches and string.
Leo's team kept disagreeing about which branches to use, and their first two bridges sagged into the mud.
Leo had built dozens of small ramps for skateboarding, so he knew how to brace a wobbly structure.
Quietly, he showed a girl on his team how to cross two branches into an X underneath the bridge so that it would not wobble.
She tried it, and the next bridge held the weight of a full water bottle.
The team cheered, and the girl told everyone that the X had been Leo's idea.
At lunch, two kids carried their sandwiches over to Leo's log and asked him how he had learned about building.
He told them about the skate park, and this time, when he added a joke, they both laughed.
That evening, Leo packed his bag for Thursday before his mom even asked.

passages.title: The Red Line
sentences: The Harbor Town visitor center held a contest for a new hand-drawn map of the town to hang beside its front door.
Sam spent four weekends on his entry, measuring streets on the town plan at the library and making sure every street was the right length compared with the others.
He colored the railway line bright red, so that visitors could find the station from anywhere on the map.
In May, the visitor center called to say that Sam's map had won, and that a designer would prepare it for printing.
Sam was so happy that he ran around the yard with Pixel three times.
Two weeks later, the designer sent him a copy of the final version.
Everything looked sharp and clean, but the railway line was now pale gray, and it almost disappeared among the streets.
Sam stared at the screen and slowly scrolled back and forth.
When his dad asked what he thought, Sam said, "It looks very professional," and closed the laptop.
Then he went to his room and did not come out until dinner.
At dinner, he pushed his peas around his plate without eating them.
His dad asked if something about the map was bothering him.
Sam was quiet for a long moment, and then he explained that the red line was the most important part, because it helped people find the trains.
He was worried that the designer would think he was ungrateful if he asked her to change it.
His dad suggested writing a short, polite message that explained his reason.
Sam rewrote the message three times before he sent it.
The next morning, the designer replied that his reason made sense, and that she would change the line back to red.
When the map was hung by the front door, Sam stood beside it for a photo, pointing straight at the bright red railway.

items.explain: Leo wanted Ana to solve the puzzle herself. He closed his mouth, sat on his hands and only gave a small clue about the colors on the wall.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that shows Leo stopped himself from telling Ana the answer.
items.hint: Find the part right after you learn that Leo knew the order. Look at his mouth and his hands.
items.explain: "He opened his mouth, and then he closed it again" shows Leo stopped himself. Sitting on his hands shows it too.

items.prompt: How did Ben feel when Coach Novak asked him to play in goal?
options: disappointed
excited
proud
relieved
items.hint: Remember where Ben loved to play. Then look at his eyes, his face and how he put on the gloves.
items.explain: Ben felt disappointed. He loved playing forward, so he looked at the ground, nodded without a smile and pulled on the gloves very slowly.

items.prompt: What changed how Ben felt about being goalie?
options: Coach Novak let him play forward in the second half.
He stopped a hard shot, and his teammates cheered.
The other goalie came back in the first half.
The other team did not take any shots.
items.hint: Find the moment Ben stopped standing with his arms crossed. Read what happened just before it.
items.explain: Ben stopped a hard shot, and his teammates cheered. After that, he clapped his gloves before every kick.

items.prompt: Put Ben's feelings in the order they happened.
steps: Ben was disappointed that he had to play in goal.
Ben was proud when he stopped the hard shot.
Ben was excited to practice in goal again.
items.hint: Find the start of the game, the hard shot and the end of the game.
items.explain: First Ben was disappointed and looked at the ground. Then he was proud when he stopped the shot and his teammates cheered. At the end, he was excited and asked to practice in goal again.

items.prompt: How did Priya feel on the eighth day?
options: worried
proud
excited
embarrassed
items.hint: Look at what Priya saw in the soil, what her face did and what she told Ms. Ortiz.
items.explain: Priya felt worried. The soil was still flat, she frowned and poked the dirt, and she said she thought her seeds were bad.

items.prompt: On the eighth day, what did Priya believe about her seeds?
options: They were bad and would not grow.
Someone had dug them up.
They had already sprouted.
They needed a bigger pot.
items.hint: Read what Priya told Ms. Ortiz.
items.explain: Priya believed her seeds were bad. She told Ms. Ortiz, "I think my seeds are bad." Really, cold nights had made them grow more slowly.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that shows Priya was excited when she saw the sprout.
items.hint: Find what Priya did right after she saw the green loop.
items.explain: "She knelt down so fast that her backpack slid off her shoulder" shows Priya was excited. It comes right after she saw the sprout.

items.prompt: How did Ben feel when Leo said, "You sped up"?
options: relieved
curious
proud
frustrated
items.hint: Look at what Ben did with his chair, the sound he made and what he said.
items.explain: Ben felt frustrated. He pushed back his chair, let out a loud sigh and said, "I always do that."

items.prompt: Why did Leo count out loud and tell Ben to listen to his sticks?
options: to help Ben stay at the same speed as the drums
to show Ben how loud the sticks are
to tell Ben that the song was over
to make Ben play faster
items.hint: Remember the problem: Ben played faster and faster. Think about how counting and listening could fix it.
items.explain: Leo wanted to help Ben stay at the same speed as the drums. Ben kept speeding up, so Leo counted and told him to listen to the sticks. Then they finished together.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that shows Ben felt proud at the end.
items.hint: Find what Ben did after they reached the last note together.
items.explain: "Ben spun around on his chair and laughed" shows he felt proud. Asking to record the song shows it too.

items.prompt: How did Pixel feel when the rover first rolled toward him?
options: excited
proud
nervous
lonely
items.hint: Look at what Pixel's feet, ears and voice did when the rover came close.
items.explain: Pixel felt nervous. He jumped up and backed away, his ears went flat and he gave a short, low bark.

items.prompt: Why did Priya stop the rover and leave it sitting still?
options: The battery was empty.
Sam asked her to take it home.
She needed to fix one of its wheels.
She wanted Pixel to feel safe and get used to it.
items.hint: Priya stopped the rover right after Pixel backed away. Think about what Pixel needed.
items.explain: Priya wanted Pixel to feel safe and get used to the rover. She stopped it when he backed away, and then Pixel crept closer to sniff it.

items.prompt: Sort what Pixel did. Put each action under the feeling it shows.

cards.text: Pixel backed away.
He sniffed the rover's wheels.
His ears went flat.
He sniffed the blinking light.
He gave a short, low bark.
His tail began to wag.

items.hint: Ask if each action came before or after Priya left the rover sitting still.
items.explain: At first Pixel was nervous: he backed away, his ears went flat and he barked. Later he was curious and friendly: he sniffed the wheels and the light, and his tail wagged.

items.prompt: Before Grandma Rose cut the pie, what did Sam think was in it?
options: strawberries and rhubarb
apples
cherries
items.hint: Look at the color of the juice, Sam's favorite pie and the question he asked.
items.explain: Sam thought the pie was cherry. He saw red juice, cherry was his favorite, and he asked, "Is that a cherry pie?" Grandma Rose only waved, so nobody told him it was not.

items.prompt: How did Sam feel when he saw the pink and green pieces inside?
options: a little disappointed
relieved
proud
lonely
items.hint: Think about the pie Sam wanted. Then look at what his grin did.
items.explain: Sam felt a little disappointed. He wanted cherry, but the pie was strawberry and rhubarb, and his grin faded a little.

items.prompt: How did Sam feel about the pie at the end?
options: He still wished it was cherry.
He liked it and wanted more.
He was too full to finish it.
He was embarrassed to eat it.
items.hint: Compare Sam's first bite with his second bite. Then read his question.
items.explain: Sam liked the pie and wanted more. After a small first bite, he took a much bigger bite and asked for a second piece.

items.prompt: How did Sam feel when he read that he had won second prize?
options: proud and a little disappointed
proud and completely calm
embarrassed and lonely
surprised and relieved
items.hint: In the second paragraph, find two kinds of clues: what Sam won, and what his shoulders and hands did.
items.explain: Sam felt proud and a little disappointed. He won a prize, but his shoulders sank and he folded the letter into a tight square. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Sam told his dad he was happy. What did Sam still want?
options: to take the tour of the train yard
to ride in the cab of the morning express
to read his essay to his class
to work as a mechanic in the repair shop
items.hint: Sam's words and his actions do not match. Look at what he did after he said yes, and what he looked at that night.
items.explain: Sam still wanted the first prize: a ride in the cab of the morning express. He folded the letter tightly and stared at a photo of the express that night. The tour was what he won, not what he wanted most. The clues are in the first and second paragraphs.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence where Sam's words and his feelings are different.
items.hint: Find Sam's answer to his dad. Look at his voice and his hands while he answered.
items.explain: "'Yes,' Sam said quietly, and he folded the letter into a small, tight square" shows it. He said yes, but his quiet voice and tight fold show he was not fully happy. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Put Sam's feelings about the contest in the order they happened.
steps: Sam was excited and worked hard on his essay.
Sam was disappointed when he read the letter.
Sam was curious and happy on the tour.
Sam was eager to enter the contest again next year.
items.hint: Read one paragraph at a time. For each one, ask what Sam's actions show.
items.explain: First Sam was excited and read his essay to Pixel again and again. Then his shoulders sank when he read the letter. On the tour he asked many questions and grinned. At the end, he had already chosen next year's topic.

items.prompt: Maya said, "Sure, it's fine." How did she really feel?
options: relieved
proud
curious
frustrated
items.hint: Do not stop at her words. Look at her laugh, her hands and her eyes in the second paragraph.
items.explain: Maya felt frustrated. Her laugh was short, she stopped talking, she pressed the edges of her cards and she did not look up. These clues are in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Why did Ben suggest playing a round with the cards face up?
options: He wanted to see Maya's cards so that he could win.
The rules said that the third round is played face up.
He noticed Maya was unhappy and wanted to help her learn.
He was bored of winning every round.
items.hint: Ben spoke right after he watched Maya. Think about what he saw, and read the reason he gave.
items.explain: Ben noticed Maya was unhappy and wanted to help her learn. He watched her for a moment, then said they could show each other their best moves. It is at the start of the third paragraph.

items.prompt: Sort the clues. Which ones show Maya was frustrated, and which show she was relaxed and happy?

cards.text: Her laugh was short.
Her shoulders relaxed.
She kept pressing the edges of her cards.
She threw both hands in the air.
She said, "Sure, it's fine," without looking up.
Her laugh was long and loud.

items.hint: Ask if each clue came before or after Ben's idea about playing face up.
items.explain: Before Ben's idea, Maya was frustrated: a short laugh, pressing her cards and not looking up. After it, she was relaxed and happy: her shoulders relaxed, she threw her hands up and laughed long and loud.

items.prompt: In the first two rounds, how were Ana's feelings and Maya's feelings different?
options: Ana was excited, and Maya was frustrated.
Ana was frustrated, and Maya was excited.
Ana was excited, and Maya was relieved.
Ana was embarrassed, and Maya was proud.
items.hint: Find what Ana did each time she won. Then find what Maya did at the same time.
items.explain: Ana was excited: she cheered and slapped the table. Maya was frustrated: her laugh was short and she stopped talking. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: What did Maya want but not say out loud?
options: to ask Mr. Varga about the green striped stone
to hold the green stone in her hands
to go back into the narrow tunnel
to show Mr. Varga her drawings of the carts
items.hint: Look at Maya's feet and her hand when Mr. Varga asked for questions. Then read what she wrote.
items.explain: Maya wanted to ask Mr. Varga about the green striped stone. She stepped toward him, raised her hand halfway and wrote the question in her sketchbook. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: How did Maya feel when Mr. Varga asked for questions in the mineral room?
options: bored and tired
curious and nervous
proud and calm
frustrated and lonely
items.hint: Find two kinds of clues: one that shows she wanted to know something, and one that shows she felt unsure.
items.explain: Maya felt curious and nervous. She wanted to know about the stone, but she stopped, looked at the floor and dropped her hand. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that shows Maya almost asked her question out loud.
items.hint: Look in the second paragraph for something Maya started to do and then stopped.
items.explain: "Maya's hand rose halfway before it dropped back to her side" shows she almost asked. Stepping toward Mr. Varga and stopping shows it too. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: How did Maya get her question answered?
options: Sam asked Mr. Varga the question for her.
She showed Mr. Varga the question she had written.
Mr. Varga saw her drawing and explained the stone.
She waited until the other kids had left and then asked.
items.hint: Read the third paragraph. Sam gave an idea, but check who walked up to Mr. Varga and what she showed him.
items.explain: Maya showed Mr. Varga the question she had written. Sam only whispered the idea; Maya walked up and turned the page toward Mr. Varga herself. It is in the third paragraph.

items.prompt: How did Sam feel right after the string snapped?
options: curious
proud
frustrated
relieved
items.hint: In the second paragraph, look at his face, his hands, his words and what he thought about doing.
items.explain: Sam felt frustrated. His face went hot, he gripped the guitar until his knuckles turned white, and he whispered that he could not play. It is in the second paragraph.

items.prompt: What helped Sam settle down after the string broke?
options: Mrs. Lin gave him a new string for his guitar.
Leo came inside and played the song for him.
He decided to sing a different song with no guitar.
He took slow breaths and found a way to play with five strings.
items.hint: Read the third paragraph. Find what Sam did with his breathing and what he worked out about his chords.
items.explain: Sam took three slow breaths and found a way to play with five strings, humming the high notes. It is in the third paragraph. Mrs. Lin offered more time, not a new string.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that shows Sam felt settled and proud at the end.
items.hint: Find what Sam did after everyone clapped. Look at how he treated the broken string this time.

items.prompt: After the race, what did Ana believe about Priya?

Priya was angry with Ms. Ortiz.
Priya wanted to run third next time.
Priya was angry with her about the dropped baton.
